title: Antibody design across observed and forecasted antigenic evolution
summary: The therapeutic efficacy of antibodies is often limited by the evolution of their targets. Designing or eliciting antibodies that withstand such evolution is challenging as their binding interfaces must accommodate antigenic variation. Here, we introduce Germinal Multi, a computational framework for  de novo antibody design and rescue that jointly optimizes a single paratope against multiple antigenic variants. We applied Germinal Multi to cancer and viral antigens, targeting both observed antigenic variation and prospective antibody escape. Multi-target optimization yielded antibodies that bound resistance-associated EGFR variants or that neutralized antigenically distinct historical SARS-CoV-2 variants, with recognition extending to variants withheld from the design process. Beyond acting on observed evolution, we redesigned the broadly neutralizing antibody BD55-1205 to restore neutralization of a prospective escape variant engineered with guidance from an evolutionary forecasting model, while preserving activity against the parental variant. Successful candidates were identified after screening tens of designs per campaign. Together, these results establish multi-target computational design as a strategy for generating antibody breadth across observed antigenic variation and demonstrate the potential of evolutionary forecasting to guide antibody redesign against prospective escape.

title: Affinity-guided design of PDZ-binding peptides in a shared latent space
summary: PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) are short C-terminal sequences that bind PDZ domains and contribute to protein localization and complex assembly. Designing PBMs could modulate these interactions while leaving most of the original protein sequence unchanged. Because PDZ recognition preferences overlap, modulating intended interactions requires considering off-target binding alongside target affinity. Computational PBM design methods generally use sequence-based affinity prediction and structure-based evaluation, but it remains challenging to guide sequence searches toward different binding objectives with a single trained model. Here, we propose a deep learning-based method to design PBMs by analytically formulating single-target, off-target-aware, and dual-target design objectives as directions in a PDZ-PBM shared latent space learned through quantitative PDZ-PBM affinity prediction. In single-target PBM redesign for DLG4-PDZ3, our method identified 100 top-ranked candidates, 84 of which were in the top 1% for experimentally measured interaction fitness in a published mutant library, compared with 64 using an existing method. In single-target de novo design of 10-residue PBMs, our method achieved the highest median in silico binding scores among the compared methods for three of the four PDZ domains tested. In off-target-aware and dual-target PBM design for PTPN3 and SCRIB-PDZ3, off-target-aware design increased between-group score differences within each domain at the cost of lower target-domain scores, whereas dual-target design yielded scores close to those of the respective single-target designs for both domains. Together, these results show that shared latent representations learned from quantitative affinities allow a single trained model to guide PBM design across different binding objectives without retraining.

title: Pallatom2: Navigating the De Novo Protein Universe with Atom-to-Atom Modeling
summary: Protein binder design requires precise coordination of molecular structure, binding geometry, and experimentally measurable performance. We introduce Pallatom2, an efficient, precise Atom-to-Atom generative model that jointly models protein sequence, backbone conformation, side-chain geometry, and target-interface contacts. A unified Atom14 representation and residue-guided sparse all-atom attention enable bidirectional information exchange between residue-level and atom-level representations, coordinating global structure with local atomic detail in a compact model of just 65.9 million parameters. Its conditioning system provides fine-grained control over binder-target engagement and global and local protein conformations, supporting diverse target-specific design requirements. In silico evaluation demonstrates broad generative capability across long-chain monomers, multi-domain proteins, and homomultimers, with monomer sampling extending to 1,600 residues. In binder design, Pallatom2 achieves state-of-the-art in silico screening performance across all nine targets with cross-method benchmark data under the reported protocols. These in silico results translate into substantial experimental success: biolayer interferometry identifies 112 active designs among 210 tested candidates (53.3%), with binders obtained for all ten experimentally evaluated targets. Six targets yield picomolar-scale apparent affinities, including K_D values of 3.96 pM for SC2RBD and 33.8 pM for PD-L1, while TNFα reaches 1.166 nM. Beyond de novo discovery, starting-interface-guided BCMA design preserves association kinetics despite substantial sequence divergence; partial diffusion improves TNFα affinity by up to 7.57-fold; and CDR-associated interface remodeling converts an inactive de novo nanobody into binders with apparent K_D values of 4.31 and 5.93 nM. Together, these results establish Pallatom2 as a versatile model for protein design, combining efficient atomic modeling, leading in silico screening performance, and experimentally demonstrated capabilities in high-affinity binder discovery, interface transfer, affinity maturation, and recovery of inactive designs.

title: Learning the limits of protein structure models with NMR chemical shifts
summary: Protein foundation models are intended to implicitly learn the chemical rules underlying protein function. However, systematically evaluating what biochemistry these models have learned remains difficult, as most downstream tasks lack experimental data fine-grained enough to expose their failure modes. NMR chemical shifts fill this gap: as direct per-atom reporters of local chemical environment, they offer a sensitive probe of structure-based representations. In this work, we present a systematically curated chemical shift dataset designed to minimize experimental confounders. We use it to benchmark diverse protein foundation models in their ability to predict backbone 15N chemical shifts, atoms that are known to be sensitive to many effects. The largest error across all models is in core residues with evidence of fast-timescale dynamics, which we investigate mechanistically using molecular dynamics simulations. Given the biological relevance of structured dynamic regions, we trained a new model based on the best of these embeddings, SLAE, to predict its own error. SLAE-ERR achieves a mean absolute error of 0.76 ppm for predicting error. Together, we hope that the datasets, evaluation tasks, and models presented here are sources of guidance for protein design model improvement.
